blocks.text: Imagine rolling a six-sided die. Each face has a number, but how do we quantify the likelihood of each result in a structured way? Enter the world of discrete random variables.

blocks.markdown: In probability and statistics, a **discrete random variable** is a type of random variable that can take on a finite or countably infinite set of values. These values are usually associated with the outcomes of a random process or experiment, such as rolling a die or flipping a coin.

blocks.title: Discrete Random Variable
blocks.text: A discrete random variable is a variable that can take on a finite or countably infinite set of distinct values, each with a certain probability.

blocks.markdown: To work with discrete random variables, we use the **probability mass function (PMF)**, which assigns a probability to each possible value of the random variable.

blocks.title: Probability Mass Function (PMF)
blocks.text: The PMF of a discrete random variable $X$ is a function $p(x) = P(X = x)$ that gives the probability that $X$ takes the value $x$. The sum of all probabilities must equal 1.

blocks.markdown: Let's consider a simple example: rolling a fair six-sided die. The random variable $X$ represents the outcome of the roll, and it can take any value from 1 to 6.

blocks.markdown: Another important concept is the **cumulative distribution function (CDF)**, which gives the probability that a random variable is less than or equal to a certain value.

blocks.title: Cumulative Distribution Function (CDF)
blocks.text: The CDF of a discrete random variable $X$ is a function $F(x) = P(X \leq x)$ that gives the probability that $X$ takes a value less than or equal to $x$.

blocks.title: Computing a CDF from a PMF
blocks.prompt: Compute the cumulative distribution function for the six-sided die roll.

steps.text: Calculate $F(x)$ for each possible value of $x$.

blocks.markdown: When working with discrete random variables, it's important to be able to determine the probability of a range of values. This can be done using the PMF or the CDF.

blocks.title: Range Probability
blocks.text: To find the probability that a discrete random variable $X$ falls within a range $[a, b]$, compute $P(a \leq X \leq b)$ using the PMF or the difference of CDF values: $F(b) - F(a-1)$.

points: Discrete random variables can take on a finite or countably infinite set of values.
The PMF assigns probabilities to each possible value of a discrete random variable.
The CDF gives the probability that a random variable is less than or equal to a certain value.
